lines.note: Tsukimairi is a monthly visit to a temple or shrine. The Portuguese definition continues with ermida on the next physical row; Tera is the Japanese institution name within that explanation.
Completes ermida dos Camis, a shrine of the kami. The pluralized Japanese name belongs within the Portuguese explanation, and the row is indented continuation text.

The entry concerns enclosing a place by building a wall or bank. The clearly printed Tçuguimauaxi has g plus ui, despite the tsukimawashi sense and tçuqimauaſu example below. NINJAL version 202510, consulted after visual reading, also records this anomalous headword; it is preserved without normalization.
Completes parede and adds a surrounding bank or enclosure. The scan reads ao redor, not the OCR's as redor; Tçuigi begins the Japanese example referring to an earthen wall.
Tsuiji wo tsukimawasu describes enclosing with an earthen wall. The Portuguese gives taipa or parede de barro; its divided final word continues below.
Completes parede de barro, specifying an earthen wall. This short indented row is part of the preceding enclosure entry.

runs.text: O ver a lũa por ceremonia, recrea-

lines.note: Tsukimi is viewing the moon for ceremony or recreation. A visible word space separates a from lũa; the printed recreation word continues on the next row.
Completes recreação and introduces tsukimi ni mairu, going to view the moon. The short Portuguese Ir a leads into the continuation below.
Completes Ir a ver a lũa, the translation of the moon-viewing example. No separate lexical entry starts on this row.
Tsukimoude is another term for visiting a temple every month. The damaged d in the headword is supported by the surviving lower stroke; the visible caron over o is retained.
Continues the monthly-visit definition: going before a kami or a Buddha. Cami and Fotoque are Japanese names embedded in Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Continuação de meſes q̃ ſe ſeguẽ hũ

lines.note: Tsukinami describes months succeeding one another. The abbreviated q̃ and nasal abbreviations are preserved rather than expanded; final hũ is masculine one and combines with a pos outro below to mean one after another.

Completes the description of successive months and introduces tsukinami no kai, a monthly gathering. The abraded initial is read as T from the remaining stem and serif, correcting the OCR's içuqinamino.

runs.text: juntamento, ou folguedo de muitos continuado

lines.note: A-juntamento means an assembly; folguedo adds the sense of a social entertainment. Both describe an event involving many people and recurring as specified below.
Completes the monthly recurrence and begins the paired expression tsukinami, hinami. Its Portuguese explanation joins months with days across the line break.
Completes Continuação de meſes, & dias: the succession of months and days. The short row is a continuation of the paired Japanese expression above.
Tsukinarabe means setting objects in an even row. The Portuguese begins with fixing several objects in place and specifies military equipment below.

runs.text: igualmente como rodelas, ou repairos que ſe v-

lines.note: The objects are arranged evenly, with shields or defensive works as examples. The final v- belongs to the Portuguese verb used on the next row.
Completes v-ſão: such shields and defences are used in warfare in Japan. Iapão is the Portuguese place-name, so it remains in the Portuguese typography.
Tsukinarashi first means flattening or levelling. The Portuguese aprainar is physically divided here, and the principal forms retain the historical -aita past ending.

runs.text: nar como terra aleuantada. ¶ Item, Tan-

lines.note: Completes the levelling sense with raised ground as the example, then begins a second sense: sounding a bell. The capital T in Tan- is visible, correcting OCR ban-.

runs.text: ger ſinos, &c. ou fazelos ſoar dandolhes com

lines.note: Completes Tanger sinos, ringing bells, and explains that they are made to sound by striking them. The striking instrument follows on the next row.
A stick or hammer supplies the instrument for striking the bells. This closes the second sense of tsukinarashi rather than beginning another entry.
Tsuki no kasa, the halo around the moon, is referred back to the tsuki entry. The cross-reference begins with the same capital T as the headword, not the OCR r.

Tsuki no katsura is explained through a dense substance or dark marking within the moon. Materia is supported by the visible t and r, correcting matenia; preto continues below without a secure printed hyphen.

runs.text: to que aparece dentro da lũa.

lines.note: Completes preto and states that the dark matter appears within the moon. The note follows the printed description without identifying a physical astronomical substance.

runs.text: Tçuqino cuma. P. i, Tçuqino cumori.

lines.note: Tsuki no kuma is marked as poetic and equated with tsuki no kumori. P. and the Japanese synonym are upright; the italic O begins the explanation continued below.

runs.text: estar a lũa hum pouco teldada, ou aparecer co-

lines.note: The moon is somewhat veiled or appears partly obscured. The printed teldada is retained rather than regularized; the comparison introduced by co- continues as como below.

runs.text: mo por antre nuuẽs, ou neuoa.

lines.note: Completes como: the moon appears as though through clouds or mist. The nasal abbreviation in nuuẽs and historical antre spelling remain literal.
Tsuki no sawari is the monthly condition glossed as women's menstruation. The initial long s in ſauari is preserved.
Tsuki no sawari ga aru illustrates having the menstrual period. The Portuguese infinitives and abbreviated plural terẽ lead into the subject on the next row.
Completes the example as women having their period. The short row belongs to the menstruation entry and remains independent physical lineation.
Tsukinuki means piercing right through with a thrust. The Portuguese construction de parte a parte begins here and is completed below.

runs.text: parte aparte, ou com lança, corno, &c.

lines.note: Completes the through-and-through sense, adding a spear or horn as instruments. The close printed aparte is retained instead of modernizing the word spacing.
Tsukikiri means cutting with a spear thrust. Its -ru and -itta principal forms are distinct from the preceding piercing verb.
Adds a stabbing thrust as an alternative to the spear stroke. This brief indented continuation closes tsukikiri.
Tsukisoi means staying close to or accompanying someone. The two circumflex-marked principal forms and abbreviated cõ are retained as printed.
Completes the companion sense and gives hito ni tsukisou, staying beside a person. The damaged capital in Fitoni is legible in context without altering the supplied reading.

The gloss identifies spirit possession or affliction, corresponding to tsukitatari. The headword is abraded between t and tari; the supplied visibly interrupted Tçuqit tari is retained as a nonblocking uncertainty rather than filling the expected a.

runs.text: em alguem, & fazer lhe mal, ou auexalo.

lines.note: Completes the possession gloss: a devil or kami enters someone and harms or torments them. Cami is a Japanese term within the Portuguese sentence.
Tsukitate first means thrusting in a sharp object. The Portuguese adjective aguda is divided across this row and the next.

runs.text: da como adaga nos peitos, &c. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Completes aguda with a dagger in the chest as its example, then introduces a second sense. Item belongs to the italic Portuguese apparatus.

runs.text: Pregando, ou fixando aleuantar algũa couſa

lines.note: The second sense is raising something upright by planting or fixing it. This differs from the preceding bodily stabbing example.
A flag or spear exemplifies something planted upright. This closes the second sense of tsukitate.
Tsukitate no mochi is freshly pounded rice cake. The Portuguese describes little rice cakes and carries feitos across the physical line boundary.

runs.text: tos daquella hora, & aßi em quentes.

lines.note: Completes feitos: made that very hour and therefore still hot. The historical aßi type representation is retained without imposing a different s expansion.
Tsukitaoshi is knocking something down by pushing. The Portuguese derrubar continues on the next physical row, which the draft had incorrectly separated as bottom furniture.
Completes derru-bar, knocking down. This is actual column-1 body text at ordinary continuation indentation, not a catchword: column 2 begins a new tsukitsumeta entry.
Tsukitsumeta hito describes an impatient or excessively eager person. The Portuguese adjective apressado is divided after a- and explained in the next two rows.

runs.text: preſſado em fazer, ou pedir algũa couſa, ou q̃

lines.note: Completes apressado: eager to do or demand something. The abbreviated relative q̃ introduces the final characterization below.

runs.text: não pode ſofrer vagar nem dilação nas couſas.

lines.note: The person cannot tolerate slowness or delay in affairs. This completes the description of tsukitsumeta hito and supplies its impatient nuance.
Tsukitsuki and tsukitsukini mean each month. The printed l introduces the alternative form and is not a Japanese syllable; the unvoiced spelling is retained.
All the months supplies the equivalent Portuguese paraphrase of each month. The short row is a continuation, not an omitted entry.
Tsukitsuranuki means piercing completely through. Portuguese parte is divided here; the instrument and through-and-through construction continue below.

runs.text: te a parte com lança, eſtocada, &c.

lines.note: Completes de parte a parte and specifies a spear or stabbing thrust. The entry concerns penetration through something, not movement across a place.
Tsukitooshi receives the same piercing-through sense as the preceding entry. The historical -oita past form is preserved.
Tsukiochi and tsukiochite describe the moon declining or setting. The headword c is abraded, but its remnant and the clearly repeated vochite support the supplied reading.

runs.text: a lũa, ou pondoſe: he modo de falar, que não

lines.note: Continues the moon-setting explanation and begins a restriction on usage. The negative não belongs with the usage statement on the following row.

runs.text: ſe vſa mais que deſta maneira.

lines.note: The expression is used only in this particular form or manner. This usage restriction applies to tsukiochi / tsukiochite above.
Tsukiotoshi means pushing or knocking down from a high place. The Portuguese adjective alto continues across the line break.
Completes alto and gives pushing as the means. Hito wo tsu- begins an example of knocking someone down.
Completes hito wo tsukiotosu. The translation describes knocking someone down by colliding with them, with an alternative manner on the next row.
Adds pushing the person as the alternative manner. The printed gap in em puxandoo is retained rather than silently merging the word.

runs.text: Lũa que aponta, ou eſtà pera ſair,

lines.note: Tsukishiro denotes the moon appearing or about to rise. The gloss also allows the moonlight preceding its appearance, as the next row explains.

runs.text: ou claridade da lũa que ſae. Vt,

lines.note: Adds the light of the rising moon and introduces the example tsukishiro ga miyeta. The Japanese word is divided after xi- at the physical edge.

runs.text: Ia ſabio a lũa, ou apareceo a

lines.note: Completes tsukishiro ga miyeta, the moon or its light has appeared. The Portuguese verb is contextually sahio, has come out or risen, but the visible lower bowl resembles b when compared with nearby italic b and h. Retain the supplied ſabio as a nonblocking doubtful or anomalous reading.
Completes the alternative as the appearance of the moonlight. The continuous claridade corrects the OCR split clarid ade.
Tsukishirome means whitening by pounding, specifically rice below. The nasal abbreviation and physical division of branco are retained.
Completes branco and gives kome wo tsukishiromuru, pounding rice white. The Portuguese pilar is divided as Pi / lar without a secure terminal hyphen.
Completes pilar bem o arroz, pounding the rice thoroughly. This closes the whitening-by-pounding entry.

runs.text: Frecha que ſe atira, ou arremeſa cõ

lines.note: Tsukiya is an arrow or dart thrown by hand. The abbreviated cõ leads into the hand as its means on the next row.
Completes com a mão, specifying a hand-thrown missile. The close printed amão spelling is retained.

runs.text: Monte feito à mão, ou artifi-

lines.note: Tsukiyama is a hill constructed by hand. The Portuguese also describes it as artificial, with artificiosamente divided across the next row.
Completes artificiosamente, reinforcing that the hill is human-made. This short continuation closes the garden-landscape term.
Tsukiyo means a moonlit night or moonlight. The two Portuguese glosses preserve the distinction between the night and its illumination.

runs.text: Coruo q̃ gralhea de noite pel-

lines.note: Tsukiyogarasu is a crow cawing at night by moonlight. The nasal abbreviation in q̃ and the printed pel- division are retained.
Completes pello luar, identifying moonlight as the circumstance of the crow's nighttime cawing.

Tsukiyose means pushing forward or bringing something closer by a thrust. Enlargement shows dotted i followed by ã in diãte, correcting OCR dũãte; the unusual ſuru principal form is visibly printed and retained.
Explains bringing something nearer by applying the hand. The Portuguese hand action corresponds to the pushing or thrusting element of tsukiyose.

Tsukizute denotes a dart or similar thrown weapon. The headword z is heavily abraded, but its surviving lower horizontal foot supports z rather than OCR c; the subsequently consulted NINJAL entry Tçuqizute independently supports the lexical identification.
Completes dar-remeſo, the contracted Portuguese phrase for a throwing weapon. The historical spelling and physical split remain literal.
Tsukizue is equated with gejun, the last ten days of a lunar month. The abraded capital G accounts for OCR Ci, while the complete right-edge dez corrects the OCR fragment de-.
Completes the last ten days of the lunar month. Here lũa refers to the monthly cycle in the calendrical definition.
Tsukizume first describes a sheath exactly matching the size and length of its sword. The damaged m retains enough strokes for the supplied headword, repeated clearly in the later figurative example.
Completes the sword-sheath definition and contrasts sorazaya, a sheath with spare length. Catana is a Japanese term embedded in the explanation; Sorazaya introduces the contrasting named kind.

runs.text: faz mais comprida pera aparecer a

lines.note: The contrasting sheath is made longer so that the sword appears larger. Catana again occurs within a Portuguese explanation, and grã-de is divided at the row edge.
Completes grande, then turns to a figurative application: tsukizumena hito. The physical-sheath contrast motivates the impatient-person explanation that follows.
Sorazaya no nai hito literally evokes a person with no spare sheath-room. The Portuguese explains an impatient person, with apressado divided across the next row.

runs.text: do, & ſofrego que não da vagar, nem deſcã-

lines.note: Completes apressado and adds eagerness or impatience: such a person allows neither time nor rest. The nasal abbreviation belongs to descanso divided below.
Completes descanso a nada, giving nothing a pause or respite. This ends the figurative tsukizume entry.

runs.text: Cara, ou focinho. Item, Parte, ou

lines.note: Tsura means face or muzzle and also a side or direction. This is an independently aligned headword, so the draft's continuation indentation is removed.
Completes the side sense and gives higashi no or nishi no tsura, the eastern or western side. The printed alternative marker l remains separate from the Japanese.
The Portuguese translates the preceding example as the eastern or western side. The clear initial O corrects OCR Deſte; soretçurano begins the next example across the row boundary.

runs.text: Couſa deßa laya, teor, ou aparencia.

lines.note: Completes soretçura no mono, something of that kind or appearance. The damaged laya retains a lower y-tail, supporting the whole word rather than OCR la a; the abraded word remains a nonblocking caveat.

Tsurakuse describes an ill-favoured or troubled facial expression. The visible b stem and following r support historical ſembrante rather than OCR ſemlrante. The gloss continues on f0491; this headword is aligned with other entries rather than indented.
